name: Jewish diaspora
scope: The Jewish conception of the diaspora as galut (exile): the dispersion of Jews outside the land of Israel read as a condition of uprootedness under alien rule, which Britannica (s1) says carries religious, philosophical, political and eschatological meaning, and which the Encyclopaedia Judaica's article "Galut" (s2) traces from the Second Temple period through medieval explanations (punishment, suffering for a purpose) to the modern 'two fundamental conceptions': that the exile must be ended (shelilat ha-galut, denial of the exile) and that the Diaspora has a right to exist and a national utility (Dubnow, Rawidowicz's essay on the concept, reviewed in s4). The sources' own range of views (Orthodox messianic ingathering, Reform mission, Zionist negation, Ahad Ha-Am's spiritual centre, autonomism) is read only as they state each as a view of the diaspora. Excluded: Negation of the Diaspora, Diaspora nationalism, Jewish autonomism, Zionism in its other strands and anti-Zionism as subjects of their own; the demography and history of Jewish communities (Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi); other diasporas.

summary: The Jewish diaspora, as the defining sources treat it, is the dispersion of Jews outside the land of Israel, read through the idea of galut (exile): a nation uprooted from its homeland and under alien rule, with a lasting feeling of alienation and yearning for the national past. The sources hold no single programme. They set out a range of views, from traditional messianic hope for the ingathering of the exiles and Reform's view of the dispersal as providential, to Zionist denial of the exile and the view that the Diaspora has a right to exist and a national use, and they agree only that Jews perceive a special bond with the land of Israel.
